content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed two strategies to generate augmented views through a pre-trained image generator. To leverage the generated view, the authors also proposed two strategies to combine the generated view with expert views (views generated by data augmentation).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

1. This paper provides theoretical analyses to support some of the claims and help the design of the method.

1. The authors conduct various experiments and analyses in this paper.

## Weakness

1. The performance of SimCLR is unreasonably low in Tab4. Since SimCLR is the foundation of all other methods in this paper, the authors should fix this issue first. Otherwise, all other numbers and experimental results reported in the paper are unconvincing.

1. In ablation studies and analyses, it is recommended to report results on harder datasets such as CIFAR-100 or TinyImageNet rather than a (nearly) saturated CIFAR-10.

1. Why W-perturb uses Gaussian noise? Why not use the strategy similar to W-search with boundary and uniformity constraints? This makes previous derivations and claims weaker.

1. To generate views offline, the authors proposed to "leverage a pretrained f". What is the pre-trained f here? If I understand correctly, this also indicates that the image encoder f should first be trained without the proposed method, generates the view offline, and then resume training with the generated views. This should be counted in the overall computation for training the model.

1. How sensitive is the model to the hyper-parameters $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_2$ for W-search, and $\sigma$ for W-perturb?

1. Why online performs worse in Fig6 and the opposite in Tab6? More results on other datasets may help clear this doubt.

content.summary_of_the_review: The major concern is the performance of SimCLR, which is the foundation of all other methods in this paper. The authors should fix it and rerun major experiments in the paper. Other critical but missing experiments are listed in the weakness section of this review.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors propose investigate the benefits of assimilating generated views with expert views to learn contrastive representations.  The authors propose two ways to create these generated views: W-search, where a search is performed around the anchor’s representation and then projected onto the GAN image space, and W-perturb, where the anchor is projected to the GAN latent space and perturbed.  The authors also propose two assimilation techniques, where either the generated views are swapped out with the expert views or a multi view contrastive loss is performed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
One big weakness of this work is inherent in its premise - what is the benefit, if we still rely on having access to expert transformations?  In other words, the assimilation does not appear to be a large gain in terms of modeling improvement.

Furthermore, whereas the authors state that their goal is to learn to generate “meaningful” views, it appears that they are learning so with access to expert transformations.

For example, the authors use the expectation of the Euclidean distances between the anchor and expert views to choose the optimal mutual information gap.  As the authors mention, the W-search method essentially tries to generate positive views whose distribution of distances from the anchor image is similar to those of expert views.

Additionally, even the generated views must have some form of expert-defined transformations applied to them (“On the generated view, we apply a weak amount of random-resized-crop and flipping”, and “applying a small amount of random-resized-cropping…also improves performance”).  Therefore, the authors propose not only learning generated views with access to some form of expert views and transformations, but to also use such expert transformations on the generated data.  This begs the question of what the immediate benefit is of applying this method - we require expensive additional models and training, but are unable to do away with expert design decisions.

A strength of this paper comes from its demonstrated empirical performance, despite the listed weakness above.  Furthermore, although the authors built heavily on existing theoretical findings, I believe they were able to tease out new insights from them to guide their work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There were no issues overall with the clarity of the writing, quality of the submission, or reproducibility.  I also believe this work to be fairly novel - although it builds of many existing theoretical works, the overall method proposed appears to be fresh in terms of the way they construct the generated views and the way they proposed assimilating them.

However, I would like the authors to double check that citations are performed correctly according to the ICLR style guidelines - I believe there are some inconsistencies (e.g. on Page 3, in the “View Assimilation” subsection).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I thought this work was interesting, and I enjoyed reading it.  However, I could not help but get stuck on the core caveat of this approach - its continued reliance on expert transitions and views, which as the authors themselves highlight throughout the work, is an existing limitation of contrastive techniques in general.  The authors seem to learn their generated views with access to such expert transitions and views, and also apply such expert transitions on the generated views during their assimilation technique.  Therefore, this begs the critical question of what really is to be gained from this model (apart from the empirical performance, which can potentially be explained by the addition of many more extra parameters/models to begin with).  It would be much more satisfying if these generated views were learned and applied without expert transition/view information whatsoever - I believe that an exploration into such approaches would be exceedingly helpful in making the case for future conference acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to improve methods that learn to generate augmentation for contrastive learning in the image domain. The authors present two methods to automatically generate data that is needed for contrastive learning, with a focus on the SimCLR framework. Experiments were conducted across 4 downstream datasets, including CIFAR10 / 100, TinyImageNet and ImageNet. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. This paper explores different methods to improve the automatic generation of image augmentations for contrastive learning. The topic is important, and could be of great benefit
2. The paper is well-motivated in the abstract and intro.
3. The authors include plenty of details for reproducing the experiments.

Weaknesses:
1. The paper proposes in Proposition 3.3 that the distances in the CL latent space could be used to represent the mutual information between the raw images. This finding does not seem to be a surprising one, since it is a wide-known exercise to use the latent space of $f$ to evaluate the capacity of learned $f$ (e.g. use t-SNE plots to visualize the learnt latent space, such as Fig. 2-b).  


2. What is the intuition that the baselines involving ViewMaker underperforms in CIFAR10/100 in general in Table 3? It would also be more comprehensive if the authors could provide original results from the paper for CIRAR10 for reference. Since the original ViewMaker paper stated that it offers comparable results in CIFAR10.

3. It would be interesting to see if the proposed method could improve robustness against common types of image corruptions, like what ViewMaker does in the paper.


4. Not sure if the linear-probing accuracy is sufficient as the sole evaluation metric. It has been shown that linear separability should not be the sole metric for evaluating representation quality, since "linear probing is not well correlated with transfer learning performance" [MAE, https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06377 ]. This suggests that the findings of this paper may not be consistent, given another transfer learning protocol.

5. How does the quality of the pre-trained generative model (i.e. how well has the $g$ learnt the data-generating distribution) affect the final performance? since the proposed method directly utilizes such a model to generate meaningful positive views.
The quality of $g$ is related to the model's expressivity, complexity of the data-generating distribution, and how well the training data covers the distribution. A most straightforward study is to ablate the effect of such additional pre-training data $g$ sees.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper could be more well-writtened. For example, there are some writing inconsistencies: e.g. pre-train vs pretrain.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies an interesting and important topic. Yet the main finding in Proposition 3.3 is not surprising, and the experimental results are a bit weak. There are some unanswered questions regarding the effect of pre-trained GAN.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to use GANs to generate augmented images that can be used for self-supervised learning. The method uses standard data augmentation ("expert transforms") as supervision. Specifically, they aim to generate augmented images such that the mutual information between the generated and raw image is the same as the mutual information between the raw image and "expertly" augmented ones. The idea is inspired by previous work which hypothesizes that mutual information is useful for quantifying the quality of data augmentations. Empirically they show that their augmentations improve SSL (as measured by linear probing and compared to expert augmentations and ViewMaker generated) on small standard datasets such as CIFAR10/100/TinyImageNet and larger scale but non-standard datasets (imagenet-scale fake images generated by GANs).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
- **Problem of interest to the community** the problem of learning to generate better augmentations is useful to the community.


**Weakness**
- **Theoretical sugar coating** section 3 is written in a way that makes it seem that there is theory backing the method, but there is really no theoretical connection between what is done and why it should be done (those are assumptions and tautologies). A much more accurate and succinct explanation of the methodology would have been: "following previous work, we hypothesize that mutual information can be used to measure the quality of an augmentation. We derive a heuristic for optimizing mutual information, which under strong assumptions can be shown to be correct". To be clear, having hypothesis/heuristics is totally fine, but making it seems as if there is theoretical backing when there is none is not. For example:
    - Proposition 3.1 and the paper use "optimal views" to make it seem that there's a  theory backing the use of such views. In reality, this is only a definition: Tian et al *define* optimal views as being those that satisfy those information constraints. This is the main premise of the paper, yet the authors provide no reason as to why one should prefer those views than any other views. 
   - Proposition 3.3 gives a (trivial) derivation of mutual derivation under the assumption that the conditional is a von Mises-Fisher and the marginal is uniform. Those are arbitrary assumptions to get the form of the mutual information that they wanted (dot product). But by making other arbitrary decisions you could essentially get any form of the mutual information you want. Eg let $\ell(z,z')$ be (essentially) any similarity you want (eg the negative of any standard ML loss) and assume $p(z'|z) \propto \exp(l(z',z))$ then $I[Z',Z = \mathbb{E}[\ell(z',z)]] + const$. So the theoretical current relation with MI is arbitrary (note that the choice of vMF in prop 3.2 is also an arbitrary decision that has no reason of holding). If the authors want to keep the mutual information perspective, they could for example say that InfoNCE is a lower bound on MI. The result is the same but at least it makes it clear that this is simply some arbitrarily loose bound. Note that MINE and InfoNCE are both just lower bounds on MI, which in your case depend on (essentially) the same variational family $f$.
    - the jump between Prop 3.1-3.3 and equation 3.1 is unclear. Why does keeping a mutual information gap (related to $\epsilon_1$), meaningful --- nothing says that you will retain the information about the labels right? Where does the uniformity constant (I suppose that to minimize information you are assuming some uniform prior)?
- **Very complex method** the method has many moving parts (GAN inversion, StyleGAN generator, optimization in generative model space...), which severely hinders the applicability of such method.
- **Unclear discussion about assimilation** I did not understand what you meant by assimilating until section 4 despite it being the center of your abstract and motivation. 
- **Unclear advantages of the proposed method** typically the motivation behind generating views is to avoid the use of "expert augmentations" but given that you still need those, I do not quite understand what is the advantage of your method/
- **Small or non-standard datasets** for a purely empirical paper I think that the experiments are too small or not comparable with previous work. The standard datasets that are considered (CIFAR10/CIFAR100/TinyImageNet) are very small and, actually, your model performs worst than previous methods for learning SSL views (eg [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00051)). Furthermore, if you are able to scale to ImageNet-scale why would you not consider the real ImageNet (instead of images generated by GANs), which is THE standard benchmark for SSL?
- **Missing baseline** AN important missing baseline is to directly use data generated by a GAN to fit the expert data augmentations.

Minor issues:
- prop 3.1: p(z) should be uniform on hypershpere which is 1/ surface area (not 1 / infinite cardinality). 
- page 4: hinge loss -> relu
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**:  the abstract, the title, and the main motivation and derivation of the loss (section 3 up to 3.1) is unclear. The rest of the paper is clear.

**Novelty**: generating data augmentations using GANs for self-supervised learning is (to my knowledge) novel, although GANs have definitely been used to augment images in other settings.

**Reproducibility**: code and hyperparameters are provided.

content.title: On Assimilating Learned Views in Contrastive Learning
content.abstract: Transformations based on domain expertise (expert transformations), such as random-resized-crop and color-jitter, have proven critical to the success of contrastive learning techniques such as SimCLR. Recently, several attempts have been made to replace such domain-specific, human-designed transformations with generated views that are learned. However, for imagery data, so far none of these view generation methods has been able to outperform expert transformations. In this work, we tackle a different question: instead of replacing expert transformations with generated views, can we constructively assimilate generated views with expert transformations? We answer this question in the affirmative. To do so, we first propose an information-theoretic framework for designing view generation based on the analysis of Tian et al 2020b on what makes a "good" view in contrastive learning. Then, we present two simple yet effective assimilation methods that together with our view generation mechanisms improve the state-of-the-art by up to approximately 3.5% on four different datasets. Importantly, we conduct a detailed empirical study that systematically analyzes a range of view generation and assimilation methods and provides a holistic picture of the efficacy of learned views in contrastive representation learning.
